question: In a small village, the probability of it raining on any one day of the year is known to be 0.22. Nico has sixteen days between breaking up and going back to school for his Easter holidays and wants to determine the probability that for at most 3 days it will be raining. Explain why it would be inappropriate to use a binomial distribution in this situation.
steps: The sixteen days are consecutive, so this is not a random sample of days throughout the year. If it rains on one day, then this will affect the likelihood of it raining on the next, so the trials are not independent.

question:
Curtis plays darts. He has determined the probability of him hitting the bullseye with one dart is 0.15. Curtis throws twelve darts. The situation is modelled as a binomial distribution.

  1. Find the probability that Curtis will hit the bullseye more than twice.

  2. Curtis throws twelve darts at three different randomly selected times. Find the probability that Curtis will hit the bullseye more than twice on one of these three times.

  3. State two assumptions, in context, that would be necessary for the binomial distribution to be valid in this case.
steps: a)
b)

c)

Curtis either hits the bullseye or does not hit the bullseye. The event that Curtis hits the bullseye is independent of every other time Curtis hits the bullseye. The probability of hitting the bullseye remains constant at 0.15.

question:

  1. Find the probability that none of the tiles Tara buys are faulty.

  2. Find the probability that at least three of the tiles Tara buys are faulty.

  3. State two assumptions, in context, that would be necessary for the binomial distribution to be valid in this case.
steps: a)
b)

c)

A tile being faulty is independent of any other tile being faulty. The tiles are either faulty or they are not faulty. The probability of each tile being faulty is fixed at 0.025.
